name: The Pork Chop

severity_by_style.why: It is the fastest way to date a Georgian-looking house to after 1930, and it sits at the corner where every trained eye goes first.
The 12-24 in returned cornice is the best-documented detail of the regional variant.
This is where the fault actually lives, and it is the single detail that separates real from applied traditional work.
The Cape's own answer is a plain 6-12 in return, so the loss is smaller - but a moulded plastic wedge is still wrong.
A genuinely clipped period return made of the building's own broad flat boards is documented practice here.
The gable carries exposed structure, not an entablature.
The rake meeting the wall in a straight line with no return is a diagnostic tell.
A plastered edge has no members to return.

symptom: At the bottom of each rake the trim swells into a small triangular or lozenge-shaped block - flat-faced, roughly as tall as it is wide, sloped on top - which closes the gap between the rake board and the eave fascia and then stops. It carries no moulding and returns nothing. It is the fastest way to date a Georgian-looking house to after about 1930.

cause.explanation: The rake trim and the eave trim arrive at the corner at different depths and different angles, and the intersection is a genuine geometry problem: the raking crown springs at a different angle from the level crown and the two must be joined with compound cuts made on site by a carpenter who has done it before. The pork chop closes the hole in ten minutes with no compound cuts, and vinyl and aluminium eave systems ship it as a stock accessory precisely so the crew never has to solve the geometry.
cause.cost_saved: $60-150 a corner in labour, so $250-600 on a simple gabled house. A properly returned cornice carrying modillions runs $400-1,200 a corner.

rule_violated.statement: A twentieth-century economy and the fastest way to date a Georgian-looking house to after 1930.
return_depth 12-24 in, carrying bed mould, modillions or dentils, corona and crown.

correct_practice: The cornice returns onto the gable wall carrying its complete profile - bed mould, dentil or modillion band where present, corona, crown - for 12 to 24 in, and then dies into the wall in a mitred return. What makes it work is that the return is a horizontal fragment of the entablature: it says the entablature runs all the way round the building and has merely been interrupted by the gable. A block that is not the entablature says nothing at all, which is why the pork chop reads as a lump rather than as a piece of architecture. In the Southern brick houses the cornice is often returned all the way round the building instead, which is a different and equally correct answer.

fixes.right: A full return 12-24 in deep in the eave's own members, mitred and returned to the wall, with the raking cornice dying into its top.
fixes.cheap: Build the return from the actual eave members - the same bed mould, the same fascia depth, the same crown - mitred and returned just 12 in. About $80-150 a corner of finish carpentry, and it is the single highest-value $500 on a traditional house, because the corner of the gable is where every trained eye goes first. Cheaper still, and historically correct: abandon the return and run the cornice LEVEL all the way across the base of the gable as a full pediment. Four corners of returns cost more than one straight run.
fixes.dishonest: An injection-moulded polyurethane 'cornice return' block or a vinyl 'pediment corner'. Both reproduce the outline at 3/4 in of projection, and the outline is not what is legible at forty feet.

test.note: A correct return projects at least as far as the cornice is tall. A pork chop is roughly as tall as it is wide and carries no profile, so it fails this and the secondary together.

secondary_tests.note: The distinguishing measurement. A pork chop scores zero - it is a flat-faced block. A correct return carries bed mould, corona and crown, plus the modillion or dentil band where one exists.
12 to 24 in before dying into the wall. Southern brick houses often return the cornice all the way round instead, which is a different and equally correct answer and passes this trivially.

detection: The single fastest check on a traditional house. Look at the bottom corner of any gable and expect one of three things. (a) The eave moulding turns the corner and runs 12-24 in along the gable wall with a shadow under it: correct. (b) A flat triangular or lozenge block, wider at the bottom, sloping on top, with no moulding on it: pork chop. (c) Nothing at all: a different fault. In a photograph, measure the return's projection from the wall against the cornice's height - a correct return projects at least as far as the cornice is tall.

exceptions.why: The clipped return is a documented period gesture on plain vernacular Greek Revival houses in the Northeast - the cheapest possible nod toward a pediment, made in the 1830s and 1840s with the same broad flat boards as the rest of the trim, and it is everywhere.
exceptions.bounds: It must be made of the building's own trim: as deep as the frieze board and carrying the crown, and at least as deep from the wall as the corner pilaster is wide. It is a SHORT return, not a wedge, and it is not a licence to hang a moulded plastic block on a Georgian.

bounds_test.note: It must be made of the building's own trim - as deep as the frieze board, carrying the crown, and at least as deep from the wall as the corner pilaster is wide. A short return, not a wedge.

exceptions.why: A cross-gable whose rake meets the wall in a straight line with no return at all is a listed diagnostic tell of the style; there is no entablature to return.
exceptions.bounds: There must be no cornice anywhere on the building for this to be consistent - a bracketed or moulded eave elsewhere makes the unreturned gable an omission again.

bounds_test.note: There must be no cornice anywhere for the unreturned gable to be consistent; a moulded eave elsewhere makes it an omission again.

exceptions.why: No cornice exists to return; the eave is 6-12 in and cut tight and the shingle field runs over everything.

bounds_test.note: Total trim suppression, verified at the casing and the corners.

exceptions.why: The gable end carries exposed structure, not an entablature.
exceptions.bounds: The rake must be 24-36 in with visible purlins or braces.

bounds_test.note: With visible purlins or braces resolving the junction structurally.

exceptions.why: A plastered edge has no members to return.
exceptions.bounds: Stucco or tile edge, no boards.

bounds_test.note: Stucco or tile edge, no boards.

inverted_by.statement: A cornice return is the fault. The cross-gable's rake must meet the wall in a straight line, and a return there reads as a Colonial Revival detail applied to an English house.
Any returned moulding is the fault; it breaks the continuous shingle field.
Where a full pediment is intended, a pair of returns is the fault - the cornice must run level all the way across the base of the gable.

confused_with.difference: The pork chop is a block that carries no profile. The other is the absence of any horizontal element at all - the rake and eave simply meet at the corner board.
There the return is real and carries the profile, and is merely too short. Here it carries nothing.
